newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore export drop stuns economists.
newsitem.headline: Singapore export drop stuns economists.

text.p: Singapore's sharp 7.9 percent fall in February non-oil domestic exports stunned economists on Thursday and some said manufacturing output could hit a 10-year low.
"I am blown out of the water. This is definitely unmitigated bad news," P.K. Basu, director of regional economics at UBS Securities said on Thursday.

The Trade Development Board said non-oil domestic exports fell 7.9 percent year on year to Singapore $5.52 billion on continued sluggish global demand for electronics products. They dropped 3.1 percent in January.
A Reuter poll of 16 economists earlier in the week had produced an average forecast of a 1.5 percent rise, but the projections varied widely from a 10 percent rise to a five percent drop.
"Manufacturing output for the first quarter is going to be very much lower and could hit double-digit decline," said Song Seng Wun, an economist at HG Asia.
He said that would be the worst manufacturing performance in the last 10 years, outstripping a drop of 3.9 percent in the third quarter of 1996.
Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at J.M. Sassoon, said he now expected first quarter manufacturing output to fall seven percent rather than remain flat as he had previously projected.
Economists said there appeared to be no escape from poor global electronics demand for the next two months.
"There has been little sign to suggest demand is going to pick up sharply," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS Standard & Poors.
Tan said hopes of an electronics recovery in the second quarter were dim.
"We would be quite fortunate to see a recovery in the second quarter. I would not be surprised if the recovery comes in the second half of the year," he said.
Liew of J.M. Sassoon said he was concerned about Singapore's disk drive sector.
"Disk drives make up about 20 percent of non-oil exports. They fell 9.5 percent year-on-year, the first negative growth in three years," he said.
Song of HG Asia said electronics exports were hit by lower prices.
"Unit prices for almost all parts and components of electronics fell 50 percent year-on-year," he said. Song said he hoped prices would even out by June.
Some economists said they were also shaving their gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecasts for the first quarter.
"I would be smashing my first quarter GDP growth from 5.0 percent originally to 3.9 percent," said Basu of UBS Securities.
But Song said he was maintaining first quarter GDP growth at 4-5 percent as construction and services, in particular the financial sector, could offset the weakness in manufacturing.
